correctness.rationale: With T the complement, any vertex having two neighbors in T is forced into T. Two occupied points fill a coordinate line, and three corners fill the fourth corner of a coordinate rectangle. Along paths in any component, a full line in an active direction propagates to the next vertex by the rectangle rule, or is already the same line when the path changes that direction. Hence the component frees every active coordinate and fixes every other coordinate. A distance-two connection between distinct components would give an intermediate vertex forced into T, so components are at distance at least three. Domination excludes the whole graph as a component. Conversely, a proper face has outside neighbors reached by changing a fixed coordinate; none belong to another face. An outside vertex can reach at most one vertex of any given face by a single change and cannot reach two separate faces. For the optimum, each T-vertex contributes at least q_*−1 boundary edges from its fixed coordinates and each D-vertex contributes at most one. A shortest-alphabet hyperplane attains |T|=N/q_*. Equality forces exactly one fixed coordinate of size q_* in each component, and every vertex outside one such hyperplane is already adjacent to that hyperplane, ruling out a second component. This proves the labelled count, including d=1 and ties of q_i. The recorded ten exhaustive subset profiles and five ILP profiles corroborate small cases; the verifier was inspected, not executed, and is not required by the proof.

evidence: Kang–Missethan–Schmid give closedness of each projection, merging within distance two under closure, and noninteraction at distance at least three. The stated setting is equal alphabets, but the inspected Appendix A proof of Lemma A.2 expands a single coordinate line then propagates it using rectangles; at distance two it first inserts a common neighbor. The connected traversal in Lemma 2.7 then merges whole faces. These steps use complete adjacency separately in each coordinate, with no comparison of alphabet cardinalities. Slivken's earlier §2 also uses repeated merging of subtori within distance two starting from singleton vertices. Tepeh covers the binary optimum and a hyperplane witness in Proposition 12 and special rook-graph results.
broader_coverage.reasoning: Replace the common K_k by K_{q_i} in the i-th slot of the deterministic face-expansion proof; line filling, the two-neighbor witness, the rectangle, and connected traversal are unchanged. This gives the same merging for the frozen mixed product without relying on the papers' probabilistic estimates. Starting with singleton faces of a closed set and repeatedly merging faces at distance at most two leaves its union unchanged and ends at faces separated by at least three. Conversely, such a union is closed.

evidence: Prior merging and noninteraction yield exactly the underlying component decomposition. For a component fixing coordinates I, every vertex of it has precisely sum over i in I of (q_i−1) edges to its complement. Separation ensures all these edges go to D. A minimum-alphabet hyperplane meets the bound and is adjacent to every outside vertex.
claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: Once the prior deterministic decomposition is translated, counting the same edges from D bounds |T| by N/q_*. Equality permits one fixed minimum-size coordinate per component; a hyperplane cannot coexist with another component, and counting the choices gives the frozen labelled number. The mixed weights add only this direct boundary count. The full classification and extremum are mechanically covered, not claimed to have been printed together in one-limited-domination terminology.

evidence: Kwaśnik–Perl's nearly perfect condition on T is that no outside vertex has two neighbors in T. Kang–Missethan–Schmid, §2.2, address exactly this closedness for the two-neighbor process; their projections are the frozen coordinate faces.
equivalent_formulations.reasoning: A set is unchanged by the two-neighbor process iff no vertex outside has two neighbors in it. Taking its complement turns this into the limited-neighbor constraint. On a connected Hamming product the additional domination condition for a closed T is precisely exclusion of T=V once decomposed into separated faces: each point of a proper face has an outside neighbor not in any other face.

originality.rationale: The central face-code structure is the closed-set decomposition for two-neighbor bootstrap percolation on Hamming graphs, with the full graph excluded. The earlier deterministic face-merging proof works coordinatewise with unequal clique sizes, and the extremum and its rigidity are immediate boundary consequences of that structure. No verbatim unequal-alphabet one-limited theorem is needed for this implication.
residual_risks: The exact publication history of the mixed-alphabet statement or its domination wording was not established. The decision rests on the concrete implication from the deterministic bootstrap results, not on an assertion of verbatim priority or on a negative search.
